Engagement and authorization:
Across the articles, engagement was most often enabled through concrete spaces and channels that brought actors into repeated contact: workshops, consultations, shared offices, living labs, meetings, websites, and co-delivery or co-evaluation mechanisms. These arrangements were repeatedly described as creating the conditions for inclusion, trust, and communication. For example, one study noted that “interactions with stakeholders took place during design workshop courses, community consultations, mentoring and internships programs” in addition to site visits and immersions (The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation: a human-centered design and shared-action learning process), while another emphasized that “creating the space and the channels of communication between the members of the group was a key aspect in guaranteeing inclusion” (Innovative Co-Creative Participatory Methodologies for a Dreamt-of Quality Education in Europe). A smaller number of studies also linked these spaces to trust-building and visibility, such as “co-delivery and co-evaluation mechanisms helped to develop positive expectations and trust” (Stakeholder salience in public sector value co-creation).

A convergent finding across the set was that meaningful participation depended on broadening who was involved and, in several cases, shifting actors from passive recipients to more central roles. Community members, service users, citizens, and other stakeholders were described as gaining voice, recognition, or empowerment: one article reported that “community members has moved from the periphery… to a central role in which they have a voice in project development” (The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation: a human-centered design and shared-action learning process), while another stated that “the service user’s voice held greater salience at this stage in the co-creation of value” (Stakeholder salience in public sector value co-creation). Empowerment was also framed as inclusion and self-esteem, as in “feeling recognized... led to an increase in their self-esteem and sense of responsibility” (Innovative Co-Creative Participatory Methodologies for a Dreamt-of Quality Education in Europe). At the same time, the evidence suggests that participation was usually multi-actor rather than narrowly dyadic: studies referred to “government, business, non-governmental organizations, civil society, and academia” (The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation: a human-centered design and shared-action learning process), “21 different stakeholders” (Revitalizing the Global Alliances for Sustainable Development: Analyzing the Viability of Sustainable Development Goal 17-A Multi-Actor Governance Approach), and “50 participants from different age groups… cultures… professions… academic fields… and socioeconomic backgrounds” (Innovative Co-Creative Participatory Methodologies for a Dreamt-of Quality Education in Europe). However, one article cautioned that “the type, number and variety of stakeholders are difficult to manage” (Stakeholder salience in public sector value co-creation), indicating that breadth itself could become a coordination problem.

Dialogue and deliberation were consistently presented as the mechanism through which engagement became substantive rather than symbolic. Across studies, actors “discuss[ed] all kinds of matters” (Co-production in digital transformation of public administration and public value creation: The case of Denmark), “came together in a weeklong workshop to help deepen their understanding, learn from each other, and develop innovative approaches” (Paradoxes of collaborative governance: investigating the real-life dynamics of multi-agency collaborations using a quasi-experimental action-research approach), or used consultations and workshops to obtain input and shape direction. In some cases, deliberation was explicitly tied to compromise or policy influence: “A topic was initiated in a debate format that would lead to a compromise and a decision” (Innovative Co-Creative Participatory Methodologies for a Dreamt-of Quality Education in Europe), and “the consortium’s input to strategic consultation exercises shaped the direction of future policy developments” (Stakeholder salience in public sector value co-creation). Decision making was often described as shared or negotiated, but not always smooth. Several studies highlighted formal forums or committees—“shared decision-making forum” (Co-production in digital transformation of public administration and public value creation: The case of Denmark) and “the steering committee, where they can decide how to cope with the issue” (Realizing public values: enhancement or obstruction? Exploring value tensions and coping strategies in the co-production of social care)—yet others showed that approval and agreement could be constrained by hierarchy or feasibility, as in “I had to play every square millimeter of text up and down the whole hierarchy to get it approved” (Public Value Co-Creation in Living Labs-Results from Three Case Studies) and “After further consultation with stakeholders, such a design was deemed logistically infeasible” (The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation: a human-centered design and shared-action learning process).

The shared value proposition was usually built through joint definition of goals, ethos, or strategy, but the evidence also shows that value was sometimes contested and had to be actively managed. Some articles described a deliberate search for common ground, such as “the search process for the common question” (Public Value Co-Creation in Living Labs-Results from Three Case Studies), “we spent a year and a half coming together and working out what our ethos and value base was” (Stakeholder salience in public sector value co-creation), and “jointly agreed-upon strategy, with a shared decision-making forum” (Co-production in digital transformation of public administration and public value creation: The case of Denmark). Others framed value in relational or ecological terms, for example defining the challenge as supporting “local economic opportunities for small-scale food producers especially women and indigenous people” (The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation: a human-centered design and shared-action learning process) or seeing nature as requiring “human and nonhuman elements… to work together and be in equilibrium” (Revitalizing the Global Alliances for Sustainable Development: Analyzing the Viability of Sustainable Development Goal 17-A Multi-Actor Governance Approach). Yet tensions were common: one study warned that “greater economic opportunities may result in environmental degradation” (The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation: a human-centered design and shared-action learning process), another noted that “the public value proposition may at times be interpreted differently by partners, or even contested and competed over” (Leading for public value in multi-agency collaboration), and several described coping strategies ranging from “accommodating, balancing, aligning, bundling, influencing, challenging, or resisting” (Stakeholder salience in public sector value co-creation) to adopting a “‘both/and’ rather than an ‘either/or’ mindset” (Paradoxes of collaborative governance: investigating the real-life dynamics of multi-agency collaborations using a quasi-experimental action-research approach).
Operational capabilities and assets:
Across the articles, operational capability was consistently described as a combination of individual and collective assets rather than a single organizational resource. Individual assets included technical skills, boundary-spanning ability, mindset, political astuteness, and practical experience: for example, one study noted that “the private sector has important resources, including innovation, responsiveness, efficiency, and specific skills” (The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation), while another emphasized that “staff’s boundary spanning capabilities were critical when securing holistic support for service users” (Stakeholder salience in public sector value co-creation). Several articles also framed participants’ capacities themselves as assets, with one social care study explicitly calling for “recognizing participants’ capacities as assets” (Realizing public values: enhancement or obstruction?). Collective assets were similarly recurrent, including start-up funds, networks, shared experiences, and complementary competencies; as one article put it, “combining their complementary resources and competencies and sharing risk” was central to collaboration (Revitalizing the Global Alliances for Sustainable Development). A related pattern was the importance of capacity mixes: most studies described value being created when different kinds of expertise were pooled, such as “students and faculty at the local university” bridging cultural and logistical gaps (The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation) or “a team of 25 young people from different ministries, local, and regional government, as well as the private sector organizations” (Co-production in digital transformation of public administration and public value creation: The case of Denmark). Only a few studies made this mixing especially explicit, so this aspect is supported but not uniformly elaborated across the set.

A second convergent pattern concerned integrative leadership and strategic management. Across the articles, leadership was less about formal authority alone than about convening, coordinating, and creating shared direction. This ranged from “the lead university’s main role is first to develop a vision” (The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation) to “the co-ordinator exercised leadership by creating a degree of consensus to achieve shared goals” (Leading for public value in multi-agency collaboration). Some studies highlighted joint or distributed leadership arrangements, such as “joint lead partners comprising two of the seven consortium organizations” managing a consortium (Stakeholder salience in public sector value co-creation) or a public servant and volunteer “tak[ing] up coordinating tasks” (Realizing public values: enhancement or obstruction?). Strategic management capabilities were likewise widely present, usually as the ability to plan, structure, and steer collaboration through processes, expectations, and stakeholder engagement. Examples included building “the infrastructure necessary to involve students and faculties ... and engage with stakeholders” (The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation), using “strategies ... to manage stakeholder expectations” (Stakeholder salience in public sector value co-creation), and making “strategic decisions to produce public value” (Public Value Co-Creation in Living Labs-Results from Three Case Studies). One article also stressed that “stakeholder engagement analyses are especially useful” for applying SDGs at project level (Revitalizing the Global Alliances for Sustainable Development), suggesting a more analytic and planning-oriented version of this capability.

The institutional and collaboration design findings were more mixed, but still showed a broad tendency toward balancing structure with flexibility. Several studies described flexibility and autonomy as enabling conditions, from “the legislation had to be simplified, made more flexible, and agile” (Co-production in digital transformation of public administration and public value creation: The case of Denmark) to “the Verschwörhaus had the highest level of autonomy” (Public Value Co-Creation in Living Labs-Results from Three Case Studies). At the same time, some articles emphasized that roles remained differentiated or bounded: “the roles of lead and local universities are different” (The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation), and in public-private partnerships “the regulatory authority is making attempts to provide information and clarity with very limited input from the substantive public partner agencies” (Sustaining Public-Private Partnerships for Public Service Provision Through Democratically Accountable Practices). Hierarchy and centrality were therefore not uniformly negative, but the balance mattered. In some cases hierarchy was portrayed as constraining participation, as when “the hierarchical structure influences the co-creation process negatively” (Public Value Co-Creation in Living Labs-Results from Three Case Studies), whereas other studies described useful central coordination, such as “the Ministry of Finance has a central position” in digital strategy co-production (Co-production in digital transformation of public administration and public value creation: The case of Denmark). Formality also varied across the studies, from informal, small-group interaction to highly mandated arrangements. Some collaborations relied on formal agreements and reporting, including “formalizing relationships with local stakeholders” through an MOU (The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation) and “mandated information sharing and engagement requirements” (Sustaining Public-Private Partnerships for Public Service Provision Through Democratically Accountable Practices), while others were deliberately less formal, with one living lab noting “this is not a plenary or something like that” (Public Value Co-Creation in Living Labs-Results from Three Case Studies).
Broader environment and public sphere:
Across the articles, the broader environment is consistently presented as something that shapes who can participate and how collaboration is organized. A common pattern is the importance of administrative architecture: studies refer to multiple levels of government, sectoral divisions, or formal multi-agency arrangements as the setting in which co-creation occurs, from “local government units in education, agriculture, and planning” in *The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation: a human-centered design and shared-action learning process* to “Denmark has three levels of governance: central, regional and municipal” in *Co-production in digital transformation of public administration and public value creation: The case of Denmark*. Similar structural layering appears in *Stakeholder salience in public sector value co-creation* (“levels often are built into constitutions, legislation, regulations and funding arrangements”) and *Paradoxes of collaborative governance: investigating the real-life dynamics of multi-agency collaborations using a quasi-experimental action-research approach* (“the Task Force Brabant Zeeland, a regional initiative of the police, the public prosecutor’s office, the tax authority, and local governments”). These accounts converge on the idea that collaboration is embedded in pre-existing public-sector arrangements rather than operating in a vacuum.

A second, strongly recurring strand concerns legislative and policy context. Several articles describe co-creation as enabled, constrained, or redirected by formal policy frameworks, whether through alignment with “government economic and human development policies” (*The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation: a human-centered design and shared-action learning process*), a “government strategy” (*Stakeholder salience in public sector value co-creation*), or explicit legal reforms such as “the enactment of the Electricity Act of 1999” and “the Public Enterprises Reform and Divestiture Act (PERD Act)” (*Sustaining Public-Private Partnerships for Public Service Provision Through Democratically Accountable Practices*). In *Co-production in digital transformation of public administration and public value creation: The case of Denmark*, the “administrative, political and legislative structure of Denmark has been changed over the years,” suggesting that policy settings are not static but evolve over time. *Innovative Co-Creative Participatory Methodologies for a Dreamt-of Quality Education in Europe* adds a supranational policy cue through “the recommendation of the Council of Europe to introduce participation,” while *Paradoxes of collaborative governance* shows how local actors may frame problems through “enforcement of zoning and administrative laws.” Together, these studies indicate that public value work is repeatedly negotiated within formal policy and legal boundaries.

Historical and cultural context is also widely present, though often as a source of friction or difference rather than straightforward support. Some studies emphasize cultural distance or contextual mismatch, such as “there are cultural gaps (e.g., language and traditions) between the lead university and targeted local communities” in *The role of universities in SDGs solution co-creation and implementation: a human-centered design and shared-action learning process* and the note in *Public Value Co-Creation in Living Labs-Results from Three Case Studies* that the labs are in “German-speaking countries with unique bureaucratic contexts and administrative cultures.” Others point to shared histories that may facilitate collaboration, as in *Stakeholder salience in public sector value co-creation* (“a history of working together”). Several articles stress that local identities and lived practices matter: *Revitalizing the Global Alliances for Sustainable Development: Analyzing the Viability of Sustainable Development Goal 17-A Multi-Actor Governance Approach* notes that “Fishing is obviously a way of life for the fishermen,” while *Leading for public value in multi-agency collaboration* describes a population that is “predominantly white” with a “small ethnic minority population and a younger demographic.” *Paradoxes of collaborative governance* explicitly highlights “differences in the historical, institutional, and political contexts in which problems had to be solved.” Overall, the evidence suggests that historical and cultural conditions are not peripheral background features but active influences on how public collaboration is understood and enacted, although the direction of their effect varies across cases.
Instrumental public values (process-orie:
Across the articles, instrumental public values were most consistently tied to process features that made collaboration appear legitimate: structured, transparent, and accountable. Procedural rationality was commonly expressed through organized decision-making, monitoring, and attention to participants’ views, whether through “shared learning and monitoring impacts” in the university-led SDG process (R1), “a structured working process with milestones” in collaborative governance (R57), or “open, objective, fair, reasonable, nondiscriminatory, and transparent” conduct in public-private partnerships (R39). Several studies also linked rationality to flexibility rather than rigidity, as in social care co-production where coordinators “lent flexibility to the process” (R22), suggesting that procedural rationality was not only about control but also about adapting process design to support effectiveness.

Procedural justice was less widely evidenced than rationality, but where it appeared it centered on inclusion, respect, and shared responsibility. The university SDG article emphasized “the sharing of responsibilities and accountability” (R1), while the education participatory methodology highlighted an “open and respectful manner” in which adults and youngsters could contribute (R45). Similarly, social care co-production aimed to increase “participation … inclusion, and diversity” (R22), and the public-private partnership article framed justice more abstractly as increasing “procedural legitimacy” (R39). A notable divergence appears in the marine conservation case, where stakeholders “were not really being properly considered” in legal decisions (R12), indicating that procedural justice could be experienced as absent even when formal decision processes were in place.

Operational control was also a recurring theme, but it was sometimes presented as enabling coordination and sometimes as constraining it. In several studies, control took the form of monitoring, audits, deliverables, or information provision: “contract monitoring meetings, quality audits” (R8), “predetermined deliverables” (R57), and efforts to provide “information and clarity” (R39). Yet one living lab case cautioned against over-specification, noting that “it is also very important … not to set goals in advance that have to be fulfilled” (R20), and the social care study described the need to “keep an eye on them while they co-produce” (R22). This suggests a tension between control as accountability and control as a potential threat to open-ended co-production.

Relational value was strongly and repeatedly associated with trust, networks, and cohesion. Trust was described as a basis for “more genuine and effective engagement” (R1), a way to “mitigate trade-offs” (R8), and a “climate of trust” that allowed participants to speak “without fear” (R45). Social networks and social capital were likewise prominent, from “formalizing relationships with local stakeholders” (R1) and “maintaining a network of contacts” (R12) to “inter-organizational relationships, networks, collaborative partnerships” (R47). Social cohesion was often expressed through bonding and shared belonging, such as “a strong and long-lasting bonding between students and communities” (R1), “a genuine sense of trying to work together” (R8), and meeting “friends and like-minded acquaintances” in the living lab (R20). Overall, the evidence suggests broad convergence that relational value emerged through repeated interaction and connection, although the articles varied in whether they emphasized trust as a precondition, an outcome, or a mechanism of collaboration.
Instrumental and prime public values:
Across the articles, democratic accountability was most often framed as a requirement to answer both upward to formal authorities and outward to partners and affected publics. Several studies described vertical accountability in terms of responsiveness to authorizers, legal mandates, or public oversight, with one article explicitly linking it to “holding governments to account” and another to “higher levels of transparency and accountability.” In co-production settings, this upward accountability was not always straightforward: one study on collaborative governance noted a “conundrum” in which collaborators may either meet organizational responsibilities or remain accountable for collaborative performance, but not easily both. A related tension appeared in social care, where citizen co-producers wanted to “trust the steering committee and project coordinators, and hold them accountable,” while also insisting that decisions not be made without consultation. Horizontal accountability was similarly emphasized across studies as responsibility to collaborative partners and external stakeholders, including “sharing of responsibilities and accountability for progress toward meeting the SDGs” and being accountable to “unfamiliar partners.”

Equal representation and inclusion was the most consistently recurring element of the theme. Most articles portrayed co-creation as requiring a widening of participation, from community members moving “from the periphery ... to a central role” to efforts to “include different types of stakeholders” and ensure “everyone is welcome.” Several studies stressed heterogeneity as a positive condition for decision-making, with one arguing that “the composition of the group should be based on heterogeneity to enrich decision-making.” Others linked inclusion to fairness and diversity in the public sphere, or to “the participatory implementation of activities and projects.” The evidence here is strongly convergent: inclusion was not presented as symbolic, but as a practical condition for legitimate and effective collaboration.

Equity and reciprocity were also widely present, though the evidence was thinner and more varied than for accountability and inclusion. Most studies framed equity of benefits in instrumental terms, showing that collaboration should generate tangible gains for participants, users, or communities: for example, “benefits through collaborative relationships with partner organizations,” “the project could bring to them,” and “These products and services created value for users of administrative processes and for citizens.” One article went further by describing the “transfer of facility ownership” as providing “immediate income generating resources for the poor and the indigenous people,” suggesting a more redistributive understanding of benefit. Equity of payment appeared only once, in the Danish digital transformation study, where it was tied to “co-financing and risk sharing among different actors and levels of government.” This limited evidence suggests that payment equity was less developed in the literature than benefit equity, and was mainly discussed as shared financial burden rather than as a broader distributive principle.
Prime public values (output-oriented):
Across the articles, prime public values were most often framed in output-oriented terms as better performance: co-created initiatives were said to save resources, improve efficiency, and deliver more effective services or interventions. Several studies linked this to concrete operational gains, such as reduced costs and improved communication in Denmark, a “highly competitive proposal” in the education case, and a solar PV system that increased electricity generation “by up to 30%” in the university-led SDG project. Yet the evidence also shows that efficiency was not automatic. One article explicitly cautioned that “collaborative practice may be ineffective or inefficient,” and another noted that it “took over a year” for a living lab to establish its own homepage, suggesting that co-creation can be resource-intensive before benefits materialize. Durable solutions were similarly associated with sustainability, continuity, and stability, from “a stable and constantly evolving platform” to “facilitate long-term partnership continuity,” although the evidence for durability was thinner than for performance and came from fewer studies.

A second, strongly convergent pattern was that co-creation was valued for its problem-solving capacity, especially through behavioral shifts and innovation. Many studies described changes in how participants acted or thought: students were drawn into “greater involvement with real-world actors and problems,” administrators “got rid of their objections toward experimentation,” and co-produced work could even shift citizens’ or professionals’ confidence, attendance, or digital mindsets. In one collaboration, fishermen eventually “allowed the scientists to accompany them onboard and test the TED devices,” while another reported that door-to-door visits generated citizen support and “informal enforcement capacity.” Innovation was also repeatedly emphasized, but usually as practical experimentation rather than novelty for its own sake: articles referred to co-designing tailored disability training, using “innovation and technology to reduce sea turtle bycatch,” and developing a “new hub model.” One outlier nuance is that innovation was sometimes described as a process condition—stakeholders’ “willingness…to join in experimentation, learning and innovation”—rather than as a discrete product.

The synthesis also shows that co-creation was commonly associated with learning, awareness, and information exchange. Across studies, participants were said to gain “valuable experience and knowledge,” “digital competencies,” and “problem-solving, creative expression, and improved oral and written communication,” while also learning from “previous general activities” or from working in “diverse teams where their point of view could be challenged.” Increased awareness was often directed at the issue itself or at other actors’ roles, such as “disability awareness training to employers,” “being aware of information and choices,” or increased understanding of “the roles of different sector players.” Data and information were a recurring enabling condition and outcome: studies referred to focus groups, surveys, interviews, performance reports, audits, and “data coherence among different authorities.” However, one article also showed the limits of this dimension, noting that the team “failed to build sufficient trust to obtain critical data from a municipality,” indicating that information-sharing depended on relationships as much as on method.
